title: Advice for Teachers Who Try Hard but Feel Hopeless
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Responding to a veteran, highly rated teacher who feels sabotaged by her administration, Stuart offers three pieces of advice. First, he argues that whole-group critiques, whether from administrators to staff or teachers to classes, are both demotivating and inefficient: the guilty feel safe in the crowd while the hard workers take the criticism personally, and both groups slide into apathy. Second, he urges cultivating excellence in oneself on the model of Atticus Finch, working with dignity because it is who one is, even in a toxic environment, and then going home to family. Third, rather than learning to 'speak the language' of buzzwords, he recommends speaking truth to power from humility and service. He gives concrete rules for doing so: be earnest, picky, timely, humble, non-evaluative and specific, and prefer face-to-face over email. He closes by noting that administrators often do not realize the harm they cause, just as teachers do not.
points: Stuart's diagnosis is that whole-group critiques backfire twice: low performers assume the problem is someone else's, while high performers internalize it and burn out.
He applies the same lesson to his own classroom, admitting he has chastised whole classes for what only some students did.
Atticus Finch serves as his model for working with excellence and dignity in an unjust environment, which he argues makes a teacher unshakeable.
Speaking truth to power means bringing earnest, specific, non-evaluative concerns to administrators one-on-one, from humility and a goal of serving students.
He assumes good faith in administrators, arguing they often do not know the damage they cause and would want thoughtful feedback from staff.
quotes: Just as it is foolish for me to chastise my whole class of students for not doing their homework last night when in fact it was only a percentage of them who didn't do it, it is foolish for administrators to chastise an entire staff for things that don't apply to the entire staff.

On the other hand, those who are trying their hardest get the impression that their hardest is inadequate (as in your case). People who work hard tend to apply the generalized critiques they hear to themselves, so when the generalized critiques seem to come despite our best efforts, the result is high stress, high burnout, and a highly toxic educational environment in which we all must, like Boxer in Animal Farm, adopt the party motto, “I will work harder.

But, as basically explained above, the psychology of low-performing people tends to be “it's somebody else's problem,” whereas the psychology of high-performing people tends to be “it's my problem.” Thus, giving critique to the whole group that should have actually been given to the low-performing group is nearly pointless.

I want to be someone who can legitimately work hard each day, know I did the best I could on that given day, know I used my time well, and then go home and be with my family. If you work for de-motivating leaders — which it sounds like you do, Rachel! — this is pretty hard.
And yet he conducted his work with excellence and dignity–even treating with dignity those who treated him with disdain.
When dealing with any administrator or superintendent, I try to put myself in his or her shoes and imagine what I would be feeling and thinking and wanting if I were them doing their job.

As crazy as it seems, administrators doing harmful things like those described in your letter often have no idea the harm they are causing, just as, every single year, I inevitably find that I have unintentionally done harm with my words and actions in the classroom.
